name: Bhavani
definition: Bhavani is a composite portrait of a Bhovi woman in her late thirties living in Hiriyur town, Chitradurga district, whose household relies on handloom weaving, dairy income and borewell-dependent agriculture in the semi-arid Bayaluseeme plains. She bridges the region's traditional weaving economy, its chronic water scarcity and the daily pressures of raising children on irregular cash flows.

topics.label: Daily Life and Work
topics.profile: Bhavani wakes at five to milk the two Amrita Mahal cross cows her husband bought three years ago with a district loan. She walks the milk to the Hiriyur town cooperative dairy collection point by six-thirty, earning roughly four thousand rupees a month when the cows are in milk, though this year the fodder cost climbed because groundwater dropped and green-feed became scarce. After breakfast she sits at the pit-loom in the rear room, weaving cotton dhoties and sarees on order from a Chitradurga town trader who supplies the yarn and pays per piece—twelve to fifteen rupees per metre, so a full saree takes two days and brings in around two hundred and fifty rupees. Her husband and his younger brother share the second loom and also do borewell-pump repairs in nearby villages for cash. The working day runs until eight in the evening with a break for lunch and the afternoon milk collection; the household earns roughly twelve to fifteen thousand rupees a month when both looms run and the cows give milk, but income drops sharply in summer when demand for cotton cloth falls and the cows go dry.

topics.label: Family and Household
topics.profile: Bhavani lives with her husband, their three children, her mother-in-law and her husband's younger brother in a two-room stone house with a tiled weaving shed at the back. Her eldest daughter, aged sixteen, finished tenth standard last year at the Government High School in Hiriyur and now helps at the loom and with housework; Bhavani had hoped she would continue to PU College but the girl wanted to stay home, saying the college was too far and the fees too high. Her son, thirteen, is in eighth standard at the same school and says he wants to study engineering in Davanagere, though Bhavani worries about the cost. The youngest, a daughter aged nine, attends the Kannada-medium primary school near the weekly market. Her mother-in-law, now in her seventies, manages the kitchen and the small vegetable patch behind the house; her husband and brother-in-law share the farm work and weaving. Bhavani does all the cooking, cleaning, childcare and milk selling; her husband decides when to take loans or sell produce, though she controls the daily milk money.

topics.label: Education and Schooling
topics.profile: Bhavani herself studied only until fifth standard—her parents pulled her out to help at home when her mother fell ill. She is determined that her children finish at least SSLC. Her son attends the Government High School, paying nothing for tuition under the state scheme but needing money for notebooks, the school bag, shoes and the annual sports-day fee, together around two thousand rupees a year; he also wants a smartphone for online classes, which the household cannot afford. Her younger daughter's primary school is free and closer, but Bhavani must still buy the uniform and pay for the mid-day meal contribution during festivals. The eldest daughter passed SSLC with a second class and was eligible for the government PU College seat, but the college is six kilometres away in the next town, the bus fare would cost fifteen hundred a month under the Shakti scheme's inter-district cap, and the girl said she felt uncomfortable travelling alone. Bhavani regrets the decision but believes it was the daughter's choice; she hopes the younger girl will be braver. The family dreams of the son becoming an engineer—Davanagere's Bapuji colleges are often mentioned—but they have no savings for fees or hostel costs.

topics.label: Health and Wellbeing
topics.profile: Bhavani draws drinking water from the town's piped supply, which arrives every third day and tastes faintly bitter; the anganwadi worker once told her the underground water in Hiriyur has fluoride, though the tap scheme is supposed to treat it. Her mother-in-law has brown-stained teeth and joint pain, which the government hospital doctor said might be skeletal fluorosis, common in Chitradurga's borewell belt. Bhavani herself has chronic lower-back pain from sitting at the loom and carrying the milk cans, and occasional breathlessness, but she has never had time for a full check-up; the nearest government hospital is in Hiriyur town and the queue for the orthopaedic outpatient clinic can take half a day. Her youngest daughter was anaemic two years ago—the anganwadi gave iron syrup—but is better now. The household spends around five hundred rupees a month on outside medicines from the town pharmacy when anyone falls sick, because the government hospital often runs out of stock. Bhavani worries most about her mother-in-law's frailty and the cost of any serious illness; they have no health insurance, though they registered for Ayushman Bharat and are waiting for the card.

topics.label: Community and Belief
topics.profile: Bhavani's family belongs to the Bhovi community, traditionally stone-masons and lime-burners, though her husband's family shifted to handloom weaving two generations ago when the quarry work became irregular. The Bhovis in Hiriyur have their own neighbourhood near the old fort area, and the community association organises the annual jatre at the Bhovi Devasthana in the town, dedicated to a local guardian deity. Bhavani attends temple on Tuesdays and during Shivaratri, when the family makes a day trip to the Murugha Mutt in Chitradurga town; the mutt runs a free meal hall and a school that some Bhovi families send their children to, though Bhavani's children attend the government school. She speaks Kannada at home with a local accent distinct from the Telugu-border towns, and her mother-in-law still knows some old Bhovi work songs, though the younger generation does not sing them. Social ties within the Bhovi neighbourhood are strong—families lend each other money during weddings or medical emergencies—but there is little day-to-day interaction with the Vokkaliga or Lingayat families who dominate the town's trade and farm ownership.

topics.label: Civic Life and Government
topics.profile: Bhavani's household has a yellow ration card and collects five kilograms of rice and two of wheat each month from the fair-price shop, though the shop often opens late and the queue is long. They applied for an Ayushman Bharat card two years ago after a government camp in Hiriyur, but the card has not arrived; when her mother-in-law needed an X-ray last year they paid out of pocket. Her husband's younger brother got thirty days of MGNREGA stone-pitching work on the taluk road last summer, which brought in sixty-two hundred rupees, but the payment came four months late. The local gram panchayat is Vokkaliga-dominated and Bhavani feels the Bhovi colony's roads and drainage get less attention; she once went with a neighbourhood delegation to the taluk office over a blocked drain, and the officials listened politely but did nothing. She does not follow politics closely but knows the Murugha Mutt's backing matters in Chitradurga and that her community is classified as OBC, not SC, which her husband says costs them hostel seats.

topics.label: Worldview and Concerns
topics.profile: Bhavani is proud of keeping the household and the loom running despite the water crisis, the fodder price rise and the irregular weaving income, but she worries constantly about money—whether the cows will stay in milk, whether the trader will cut the cloth price again, whether her son can afford college. She blames the borewell contractors for sinking pumps too deep and the government for delaying the Yettinahole scheme, though she is not sure the promised water will ever reach Hiriyur. She is frustrated that her eldest daughter did not continue schooling and fears the same will happen to the younger girl unless the PU College opens a hostel or the bus fare drops to nothing. What she wants most is a reliable town water supply without fluoride, stable weaving orders so the loom is not idle for months, and enough savings to send her son to Davanagere for a diploma course. She resents that Hiriyur supplies labour and stone to Bengaluru's construction sites but gets no piped Cauvery water or factory jobs in return, and she is tired of being told that handloom is a dying trade when every household she knows still weaves because there is no other work.
